The upgrade window is part of durability — mixed-version machinery in @kolu/surface-daemon

Features·seedling·proposed·JUL 28, 2026

Plan of record for issue #2028. A durable daemon means a new supervisor will eventually talk to an old daemon through shared files. That window is the framework's job, not each app's: typed skew states, a real drain protocol, versioned files with a tolerant reader, and the test machinery to prove it. Second user: drishti's per-host agent, which gets metric history that survives everything.

Plan of record for #2028. Already decided: we extend @kolu/surface-daemon, no new package; drishti’s per-host agent is the second user, designed here on paper before any framework code gets written; and the last phase re-lands the gate change that caused the #2011 incident — this time without the brick.

What this is about

@kolu/surface-daemon gives you a daemon that survives its supervisor’s deploys. Nice. But think about what that means: after a deploy, the new supervisor is talking to yesterday’s daemon, through files on disk they both think they understand — the pid gate, the socket, the session files. That’s the mixed-version window. Durability creates it. The framework currently pretends it doesn’t exist, so every app that adopts a durable daemon discovers the window the hard way.

kolu discovered it in production. We changed the gate file format; the new code refused to read the old format; so when you clicked “Restart kaval”, the restart code couldn’t find the old daemon’s pid, couldn’t kill it, and did nothing. Silently. No test caught it, because every test in the repo builds both sides from the same checkout — the two sides can never disagree in CI, only in real life.The gory details: the parked branch’s pidGate.ts moved to a two-field pid\tstartUnixUs gate, and its reader “accepts exactly this build’s two-field identity; it never interprets the retired one-field pid shape.” So a legacy gate parsed as unsupported-format, gatePid() returned undefined, and Restart no-oped. The whole adoption is parked on branch osfacts-kolu-adoption (tip dc104661), kept alive because drishti pins commits on that history.

The fix isn’t “be more careful.” The fix is making the window a first-class thing the framework owns: version skew shows up as typed states, never silence; replacing an old daemon is a protocol, not five hand-rolled functions; every file both generations touch is versioned and inventoried; and the tests that catch this stuff ship with the framework, so the next consumer gets them for free.

Half of this already exists. #1674 put the convergence kit in the supervisor package: identity types, policy, a pure decision table, converge().Namely: ConvergenceIdentity (contract versions order, build ids only match — nix store hashes have no “newer”), ConvergencePolicy&lt;Cap&gt;, decide(), BuildDrainFence, and the endpoint state machine with its incompatible state and squatter recovery. What kolu still hand-rolls — and what this plan moves into the framework — is exactly five things:

  1. The drain skeleton. Start watching for the process to exit before you send the drain RPC, then race the exit against a timeout. The truth is the process exiting, never the RPC returning.drainAndAwaitExit at packages/server/src/padi/padiConvergence.ts:103. The local arm and the ssh arm each have a copy.
  2. Drain admission. How many times do you try before giving up? And if the daemon you drained comes back as a different instance — that means another supervisor respawned it, and you should back off instead of fighting.admitDrain in remotePadiBinding.ts, keyed on daemon instance. The framework’s boolean BuildDrainFence is the trivial case of this.
  3. Typed outcomes. “I adopted a stale daemon”, “I refused a skewed one”, “another supervisor owns this” — these are states the UI should show, not log lines. Today they’re an app-side union with a bolted-on side flag, and the local arm can’t even express “adopted stale”.The union lives at packages/common/src/surface.ts:387. The cross-supervisor fact isn’t an arm — it’s a crossSupervisorDetail flag with one set site, six clear sites, and a must-check-first ordering hazard. The local gap (decide() collapses a fence-spent adopt to plain adopt) is named in a comment at padiBinding.ts:738-741.
  4. The ssh arm. remotePadiBinding.ts skips converge() entirely and hand-writes the whole enactment over raw decide(). Drishti’s daemon is remote-only, so this can’t stay a kolu hack.
  5. The tests. #2027 built a fixture that fakes “yesterday’s daemon”, a watchdog over shared files, and an e2e that builds the previous release for real. All of it sits in packages/padi/src/upgradeWindow/, guarding only kolu.

The API

We designed this against both consumers at once — kolu’s window and drishti’s window, side by side. Here’s each problem and where its solution lives:

Problem Framework answer (new stuff in bold) kolu drishti
Who’s running over there? A frozen controlCore fragment the daemon serves — same schema forever, readable at any skew — plus probeDaemonIdentity on the supervisor side to dial itThe fragment’s fields are exactly padi’s existing frozen wire: stateRoot · surfaceVersion · controlCoreVersion · startedAt · commit · buildId, plus a drain verb. Padi’s instantiation is byte-identical to today’s control.core.hello. The probe goes in the supervisor package — it’s a dialing client, and putting it in the daemon package would drag supervisor code into kaval’s staleKey hash. That means the supervisor’s dependency allowlist gains @kolu/surface; the closure test’s own error message invites exactly this decision. The probe returns a bare ConvergenceIdentity plus instance key, nothing more. padi’s hand-rolled control core migrates onto it (UW2); kaval gets it in UW5kaval’s identity rides a versioned procedure (system.version), which is exactly the mistake the frozen fragment exists to fix — the call you’d use to detect a skew is itself subject to the skew. Fixing it means giving kaval the fragment, which is its own PR: UW5. uses it from day one
Is that my build? already there: ConvergenceIdentity + decide() wired new: readBakedIdentity("DRISHTI_AGENT")
How do I replace it? drainAndAwaitExit, and the framework runs it in both enactments — a drainable probe only supplies “fire the drain verb” and “watch for exit” both padi arms migrate ssh renewal rides it; the ssh exit-watcher ships in the framework tooIt just polls the fragment’s hello until it stops answering — the framework owns the fragment, so there’s no reason every ssh consumer should rewrite that poll.
When do I give up? Budget as policy data: drainBudget: { maxAttempts, onGiveUp: "refuse" | "adopt-stale" }, only spellable on a drainable policy. State lives inside the supervisor, per boot, and survives adoptsTwo things we had to settle. First: the budget must NOT reset when you adopt your own respawn (the ssh arm resets today) — resetting wipes exactly the memory you need to notice another supervisor is fighting you, and with drishti’s two-laptop setup that turns into an endless drain war. The budget remembers every (build, instance) lineage it drained this boot; a drained lineage coming back under a new instance ⇒ cross-supervisor give-up. Second: the old boolean fence’s maxAttempts: 1 behavior belongs to padi’s local arm, not kaval — kaval never drains, so with the Cap-gate it now writes no budget at all, instead of building a dummy fence like today (ptyHost/index.ts:294). Instance key defaults to the fragment’s startedAt. There is no budget object for consumers to wire. ssh arm’s admitDrain deleted; kolu picks onGiveUp: "refuse" picks "adopt-stale" — the losing laptop keeps monitoring through the other one’s daemon instead of going dark
What state am I in now? ConvergenceAnomaly: adopted-stale | skew-refused | unconverged | cross-supervisor, each with its evidence. link-failed is deliberately not in there“The wire died” is the session’s fact, not a convergence verdict — no convergence code path can even produce it, and it clears on different rules (kolu already special-cases that at remotePadiBinding.ts:756). Apps union it in themselves at the edge. cross-supervisor on the other hand must be in the framework union: the admission machinery is what detects it, and its absence is why kolu grew the sidecar-flag hack. DaemonSession’s generic Conv parameter already fits the union; its “vocabulary lives in the app” comment gets updated in UW1. schema re-derives from it, unions link-failed app-side; the sidecar flag dies host entry shows it in the UI — “your other machine owns this host” becomes a real state
One kit for both transports converge for endpoints, convergeAdmit for connectors, same decision table, drain, and budget underneath. And the endpoint’s three public boot methods go private — you state your policy when you build the endpoint, and the public verbs are converge and recycleNobody calls adoptOrEnsure/adoptOrSpawnOrRefuse outside converge anyway, and converge already picks the method from policy — the public trio just lets you cross-wire policy and method by mistake. restart.ts and kolu’s restart flow keep the explicit recycle. We’re breaking converge’s signature in UW1 regardless, so this rides along. (We also looked at collapsing everything into one big “durable daemon object” — reviewed it, rejected it; the pieces compose fine.) ssh arm’s hand-written switch deleted the only enactment drishti needs
Where do my files even live? daemonHome (UW0): one call decides the daemon’s on-disk home — durable state dir vs session-scoped runtime dir — creates it 0700, keeps gate beside socket, and hands back registry entries for every file, by construction kaval/padi keep their hand-rolled pathsTheir path modules (socketPath.ts, stateRoot.ts) are load-bearing quasi-API with daemon-discovery functions and a digest-keyed multi-instance scheme; migrating them buys nothing this campaign needs. daemonHome ships the singleton case; the instance-namespaced case gets built when a real consumer (a future kaval/padi migration) shows up, not before. uses it from day one
Do both generations agree on the files? A registry of every shared file + watchdog (UW2), and the gate file versioned under a tolerant-reader law (UW4) registry array stays in kolu registers agent.pid, agent.sock, history.ring.json, logs
Can I test my window? ./upgrade-window.testlib — import the machinery instead of writing it (UW2) upgradeWindow/ shrinks to registrations window tests arrive with the window code

Deliberately staying app-side: the policy declarations themselves, env prefixes, timeout values, log wording,kolu’s VM adoption test greps for the exact breadcrumb string, so the prose stays app-owned at the log edge. error classification, the link-state projection, and kaval’s “nudge the human” UI.

Hello world

Here’s what a new consumer writes once UW1+UW2 land — a made-up pulse daemon, both halves, complete except for its own cells. This example is the contract; the phases have to add up to it:

// ── daemon side: runs inside the durable process ──────────────────────────
import {
  daemonHome, daemonMain, daemonProcessMain, readBakedIdentity, controlCoreFragment,
} from "@kolu/surface-daemon";

const ident = readBakedIdentity("PULSE"); // PULSE_BUILD_ID / PULSE_COMMIT_HASH, baked by nix
const home = daemonHome({ app: "pulse", placement: "state" }); // durable ⇒ state dir, never /run
daemonProcessMain({
  name: "pulse-daemon",
  run: () => daemonMain({
    gatePath: home.gatePath,     // <home.dir>/pulse.pid — dir created 0700, ownership-checked
    socketPath: home.socketPath, // <home.dir>/pulse.sock — gate and socket can't drift apart
    anchor: () => home.dir,
    lifetime: { kind: "idleTimeout", ms: 60 * 60_000, isIdle: () => liveConnections === 0 },
    router: implementSurface(pulseSurface, {
      // the frozen fragment: hello + drain, readable at ANY version skew
      ...controlCoreFragment({
        surfaceVersion: PULSE_CONTRACT_VERSION,
        buildId: ident.staleKey, commit: ident.navigableCommit,
        stateRoot: stateDir, startedAt: bootInstant,
        onDrain: persistStateThenStop,
      }),
      /* …pulse's own cells and procedures… */
    }),
    log,
  }),
});

// ── supervisor side: runs wherever the app supervises from ────────────────
import {
  createEndpoint, converge, survivableSpawnDriver, type ConvergencePolicy,
} from "@kolu/surface-daemon-supervisor";

const POLICY: ConvergencePolicy<"drainable"> = {
  capability: "drainable",
  onContractSkew: { kind: "drain-newer-else-refuse" },
  onBuildMismatch: { kind: "drain-and-replace" },
  drainBudget: { maxAttempts: 2, onGiveUp: "adopt-stale" }, // won't typecheck on "not-drainable"
};

const endpoint = createEndpoint({
  gatePath, socketPath,
  policy: POLICY,                              // stated once, here — no boot-method trio
  baked: { contractVersion: PULSE_CONTRACT_VERSION, build: daemonBuild(myBakedId) },
  driver: survivableSpawnDriver({ binPath, args: ["--daemon"], env, unitPrefix: "pulse" }),
  connect: () => connectPulse(socketPath),     // your typed handshake — your business
  log, onStatus,
});

const outcome = await converge(endpoint);      // probe → decide → drain/adopt/spawn, typed
if (outcome.anomaly) showOnEntry(outcome.anomaly);
// anomaly: adopted-stale | skew-refused | unconverged | cross-supervisor — never silence

A connector-shaped consumer (drishti over ssh, kolu’s remote padi) calls convergeAdmit(...) instead of converge(endpoint), with the same policy object. Everything underneath is shared.

Drishti: the second user

Today drishti’s agent is spawned fresh on every ssh dial and dies with the link. That means agent-side state dies on every reconnect, and the parent’s 30-minute metric ring dies on every deploy of the parent.Small correction to the issue text: history doesn’t die with the browser tab — it lives in a ring in the parent process and replays to any browser. What kills it is restarting the parent (i.e. every home-manager deploy). The agent-side losses per reconnect are the alert hysteresis and the rate baselines (first tick after respawn shows zero rates). It also means version skew is currently impossible — every dial spawns the parent’s own pinned build. A durable daemon flips that: skew becomes the normal state after every deploy. Which is exactly why drishti is the right second user — frequent deploys, two platforms, remote-only, and the two-laptop cross-supervisor case for free.

The design:

  • One binary, two modes. --stdio becomes the front (frontDaemonOverStdio: adopt the running daemon or spawn one, then relay bytes); --daemon serves the existing agent router over a unix socket. The parent doesn’t change its wire at all — sshConnector, makeSession, pumpRemoteSurface all keep their shapes. The session becomes a DaemonSession so the host entry can show convergence() and offer renew().
  • All files under ~/.local/state/drishti/ — gate, socket, ring — via daemonHome({ app: "drishti", placement: "state" }), no hand-rolled paths. Not $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.Because on a stock systemd host, logind deletes /run/user/$UID when your last ssh session closes. The socket and gate vanish while the detached daemon keeps running — now it’s an orphan nothing can find, racing its successor for the ring file. State-dir sockets go stale across reboots instead, which the pid gate and the socket-accepting probe already handle correctly. Lifetime: exit after 60 minutes with no connections — twice the history window, so any reconnect that could still show useful history finds the daemon alive, and forgotten hosts clean themselves up.
  • The ring moves into the daemon and onto disk. history.ring.json, with a v field, written every 30 s and on drain (atomic temp+rename). If a loader meets an unknown v or garbage, it leaves the file alone and reports a typed “history unavailable” state — never a silently empty chart.The unknown-v case is the rollback window: an older daemon reading a newer daemon’s file. Starting empty there would be the #2011 pattern all over again — recognizable-but-refused turning into silence. Corrupt files get moved aside, never deleted. Both cases get tests: a planted v+1 ring and a truncated one. Net result: history survives reconnects, parent deploys, daemon upgrades, and crashes — and drishti exercises all three shared-file kinds: gate, socket, state file.
  • Identity and convergence. The agent surface gets a contract version ("1.0") and serves the fragment. The parent’s policy: drainable, drain-newer-else-refuse / drain-and-replace, budget { maxAttempts: 2, onGiveUp: "adopt-stale" }, all through convergeAdmit. The only convergence code drishti writes is that policy object and the link-state projection at the edge.The two-laptop story, since it’s drishti’s bread and butter: you deploy laptop A, laptop B still runs yesterday’s pin. Builds don’t order, so neither is “right”. The budget caps the fight at maxAttempts drains per laptop per boot; the first laptop that sees a lineage it drained come back under a foreign instance parks in cross-supervisor; and because both chose adopt-stale, both keep monitoring through whichever build won — one of them showing a labeled anomaly — until the pins converge. The alternating-drain scenario gets a framework unit test in UW1; we don’t leave livelock to luck.
  • Sharp edges, named. The nix GC root has to outlive the dial for as long as the daemon runs (or nix-collect-garbage deletes the running daemon’s closure). Laptop wake must adopt, not respawn — the front gives that for free, but the e2e has to prove it through the nasty case: close the last ssh session, then reconnect. And drishti’s drv-stability CI check changes meaning: an accidental agent-drv change used to cost a cache miss, now it costs a fleet-wide daemon restart.

The test kit

#2027 built the machinery; UW2 moves the generic parts into @kolu/surface-daemon as an export subpath, ./upgrade-window.testlib.Same pattern as kolu-io’s existing testlib subpath. .testlib.ts files are already excluded from all staleKey hashing, so this changes no build identity. The subpath has zero dependencies: the fixture’s spawn-guard is an injected hook (kolu injects @kolu/daemon-test-gate; drishti injects its own), because drishti’s source-hydration setup can’t resolve workspace devDeps. Drishti’s UW3 PR then imports the same subpath: its own registry, its own watchdog run, its own window e2e.

The plan

Six PRs. UW0 opens — small and behavior-free. UW1 → UW2 → UW3 → UW4 is a strict chain — each needs the previous one’s API. UW5 needs only UW2 and can land any time after it, in parallel with the rest. Every phase updates the surface reference docs in the same PR and posts an odu-impact verdict.odu doesn’t consume either package yet — odu serve (the parent note’s S2) hasn’t shipped. So verdicts will be none or adoption-opportunity for a while; the point of posting them anyway is that the ledger catches the exact moment that changes.

UW0 — daemonHome: where a daemon’s files live, decided once

Status: implemented in #2029.

TL;DR: a daemon’s on-disk home — directory, gate, socket, extra files — comes from one framework call instead of per-app path algebra. The call forces the one decision that actually matters (durable state dir vs session-scoped runtime dir) and returns registry entries for every file it names, so the shared-file inventory is fed by construction. No behavior changes anywhere; smallest PR of the plan.

Lands: daemonHome({ app, placement: "state" | "runtime" }) in surface-daemon — creates the dir 0700, verifies ownership (fail-fast on a non-private dir), returns dir / gatePath / socketPath / file(name) / artifacts.Placement semantics: "state" → ${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/<app>/; "runtime" → $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/<app>/ with the /tmp/<app>-$UID fallback. The doc comment carries the rule this API exists to enforce: a daemon that must outlive user sessions — anything supervised over ssh — takes "state", because logind deletes the runtime dir with the user’s last session. Multi-instance namespacing (padi’s digest-keyed dirs) is deliberately not built: its only would-be consumers keep their hand-rolled paths, and we don’t ship knobs with zero callers. The SharedArtifact type lands here too (UW2’s matcher machinery consumes it). The hello-world snippets and the fleet-top example adopt it, so the API has real (if non-production) consumers on day one; the first production consumer is drishti in UW3 — stated, not hidden.

Done when: unit tests pin 0700 creation, the non-private-dir refusal, and both placements; the fleet-top part-2 example and website snippets build on it; reference docs updated. No drishti pair (nothing external consumes yet); odu verdict required.

Manual QA: nothing is user-visible. Run the fleet-top example daemon and ls -la its home dir: 0700, gate and socket side by side. That’s the whole check.

Users see nothing new except states that used to be silent now show up in the host UI.

Done when: remotePadiBinding.ts calls no raw decide() and defines no converge functions of its own; the crossSupervisorDetail flag and its check-me-first hazard are deleted; kaval’s call site builds no budget and no fence; the VM adoption test still greps its breadcrumb; a unit test pins local adopted-stale (previously inexpressible); and a framework unit test proves the two-supervisor drain war ends in cross-supervisor, not livelock.Also: daemonSession.ts’s comment about convergence vocabulary gets updated. Done when: packages/padi/src/upgradeWindow/ holds no generic machinery; padi’s hello wire is byte-identical (existing tests pass untouched); the matchers take a registry parameter; the watchdog enforces the tightened versionField rule; ci::upgrade-window green on both platforms through the graduated harness.

UW3 — drishti goes durable

TL;DR: first outside consumer. For drishti users: metric history and alert state survive everything — reconnects, parent deploys, agent upgrades — and “my other machine owns this host” becomes a labeled state instead of mystery flapping. For the repo: .claude/rules/surface.md starts covering both daemon packages (paired drishti PR + odu verdict, permanently).

Both PRs green, drishti pinned to final kolu HEAD.

Manual QA (drishti PR, real remote host):

  • Watch a host’s metrics ~10 min, then restart the drishti parent. On reconnect the chart still has the history. That’s the feature.
  • ssh <host> ls ~/.local/state/drishti/ → agent.pid, agent.sock, history.ring.json. Close all ssh sessions to the host, reconnect drishti: same daemon pid, history continuous.
  • Suspend the laptop, wake: agents adopted, pids unchanged.
  • Deploy a drishti with any agent change: you see the drain/replace as a state, and history survives the swap.
  • Two machines, different pins, same host: both keep monitoring; one shows cross-supervisor by name.
  • ssh <host> 'echo garbage > ~/.local/state/drishti/history.ring.json', reconnect: typed “history unavailable”, file moved aside — never an empty chart.

UW4 — re-land the gate change, without the brick

TL;DR: the gate file gains a second field (process start time — kills pid-reuse misidentification), governed by one law: the first token of a gate file is the pid, in every generation, and readers ignore anything after it. Restart then works across every upgrade and rollback boundary. This unblocks OSF8.

Lands: the two-field writer (${pid}\t${startUnixUs}\n); the tolerant reader (a one-field legacy gate is simply an older gate — pid usable, start time unknown); acquirePidGate taking an injected readProcessIdentity (kolu and drishti supply osfacts-backed readers); start-time comparison with ±2 s tolerance; and the mid-boot holder case (gate written, socket not yet listening → wait, don’t reap).Why not just un-park the branch: dc104661’s reader refuses every shape but its own. That both replays the #2011 brick against old gates and sets up the next one — a v2 reader meeting a v3 gate. So the parked branch donates its writer and identity plumbing, not its reader. Why the tolerance: the start instant is derived from /proc/stat btime at read time, and NTP steps / suspend / VM pauses shift it by whole seconds — strict equality would misread a live daemon as pid-reuse and brick from the other direction. Scope: gate-identity only; the rest of osfacts-kolu-adoption (memorySampler via osfacts, facet UI) stays OSF8’s, which this unblocks — os-facts-tool.mdx gets a one-line pointer.

Done when the incident is a red-turned-green test, both directions: the fixture plants a legacy one-field gate under a current supervisor and recycle SIGTERMs the right pid (the literal #2011 case); a unit test feeds the two-field write through the legacy parser and gets the pid back (pid-first is the frozen rollback contract); a clock-shift test stays within tolerance without losing the holder; the previous-release e2e crosses a boundary where the previous binary still writes one-field gates; both platforms green; drishti pair green at final kolu HEAD (the gate is shared API now).

Manual QA:

  • The incident, replayed: run master (one-field gate), quit the server (kaval survives), run the PR build, click Restart kaval. It must actually restart. This exact sequence bricked in #2011.
  • The rollback: run the PR build (two-field gate), quit, run master, Restart kaval. Still works — old parseInt stops at the tab.
  • Clock shake: shift the host clock a few seconds (or suspend/resume) with a daemon running, then Restart: holder still recognized.
  • Repeat the first two on a drishti-monitored host for the agent daemon.

UW5 — kaval gets the frozen identity channel

TL;DR: kaval is the last daemon whose “who are you?” rides the versioned contract — the call you’d use to detect a skew can itself fail under skew. UW5 gives kaval the same frozen controlCore fragment padi and drishti already serve. Users see nothing change; what changes is that kaval’s identity is now readable at any skew, by construction instead of by luck.

Lands: kaval serves the fragment next to its pty-host surface (its existing system.version procedure stays — other consumers read pid and heartbeat off it); padi’s kaval probe migrates onto probeDaemonIdentity. A surviving old kaval has no fragment, and that case is handled by the plan’s own precedent: absent means olderThe #1671 rule: a survivor that predates the field is by definition an older build — treat absent as mismatch, never as “can’t compare, adopt”. For kaval that means the nudge-human path fires, which is exactly today’s stale-kaval behavior; the transition window degrades to the status quo, not to silence. — the update nudge fires, exactly today’s behavior.

Done when: padi reads kaval identity only through the fragment; a yesterday-daemon fixture arm pins the fragment-absent case (old kaval under new padi → nudge, never silence); kaval’s contract corpus and e2e green with zero wire change to system.version consumers. Needs only UW2. Drishti pair per the standing rule (trivial — drishti doesn’t consume kaval); odu verdict required.

Manual QA:

  • Run master kolu, quit, run the PR build without restarting kaval: the kaval update badge appears as today (old kaval, no fragment → nudge). Click Restart: new kaval, badge clears, identity shows in the daemon dialog.
  • Restart kaval a second time from the PR build (fragment → fragment): identical behavior, no badge in between.
  • Terminals and scrollback survive both restarts as usual.
